title: German Basics: Greetings & the German-Speaking World
description: Your first steps in German — greet people, introduce yourself, say where you live, count to 100, pronounce the special letters, and meet the German-speaking countries.

notes.heading: 📌 Greetings & Goodbyes (Begrüßungen)
notes.body:
German has greetings for different times of day and different levels of formality.

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Guten Morgen | Good morning |
| Guten Tag | Good day / hello (formal) |
| Guten Abend | Good evening |
| Gute Nacht | Good night (when going to bed) |
| Hallo | Hello (informal, any time) |
| Wie geht es dir? | How are you? (informal, to one person) |
| Wie geht es Ihnen? | How are you? (formal, to adults/teachers) |
| Mir geht es gut, danke. | I am fine, thank you. |
| Auf Wiedersehen | Goodbye (formal) |
| Tschüss | Bye! (informal) |
| Bis später / Bis bald | See you later / See you soon |

Use **du** and informal phrases with friends and family; use **Sie** (Ihnen) and formal phrases with teachers, shop assistants and adults you do not know well.

notes.heading: 🔑 Introducing Yourself
notes.body:
To say who you are and ask others:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Ich heiße Anna. | My name is Anna. (literally: I am called Anna) |
| Mein Name ist Anna. | My name is Anna. |
| Wie heißt du? | What are you called? |
| Und du? | And you? |
| Freut mich! | Pleased to meet you! |
| Woher kommst du? | Where do you come from? |
| Ich komme aus England. | I come from England. |

A full mini-dialogue:
— Hallo! Wie heißt du?
— Ich heiße Ben. Und du?
— Ich heiße Lena. Freut mich!
— Freut mich auch!

Notice **heißen** changes its ending: ich heiß**e**, du heiß**t**. The verb ending tells you who is speaking.

notes.heading: 🔑 Saying Where You Live
notes.body:
Use the verb **wohnen** (to live):

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Wo wohnst du? | Where do you live? |
| Ich wohne in London. | I live in London. |
| Er wohnt in Berlin. | He lives in Berlin. |
| Sie wohnt in Wien. | She lives in Vienna. |

Conjugation of **wohnen** in the singular:
- ich wohn**e** — I live
- du wohn**st** — you live
- er/sie/es wohn**t** — he/she/it lives

The pattern is: verb stem (wohn-) + ending (-e, -st, -t). This pattern works for most regular German verbs, so it is worth learning now. In a German sentence the verb is almost always the **second idea**, even if the sentence starts with another word: *In London wohne ich seit drei Jahren.* (In London I have lived for three years.)

notes.heading: 📌 The German-Speaking World (D-A-CH)
notes.body:
German is not only spoken in Germany! The three main German-speaking countries are often called **D-A-CH**:

| Country | Capital | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **D**eutschland (Germany) | Berlin | About 84 million people |
| **A**ustria (Österreich) | Wien (Vienna) | About 9 million people |
| **CH** — die Schweiz (Switzerland) | Bern | German is one of four official languages |

German is also an official language in Luxemburg (Luxembourg), Liechtenstein and parts of Belgien (Belgium), and is widely understood in Südtirol in northern Italien (Italy). Altogether more than 100 million people speak German as a first or second language.

Watch out: die Schweiz is a **feminine** country name, so it keeps its article — *Ich komme aus der Schweiz.* Most countries (Deutschland, Österreich, England) use no article: *Ich komme aus Österreich.*

notes.heading: 🔑 Numbers 0–100 (Zahlen)
notes.body:
**0–12** just have to be learned:

| 0 null | 1 eins | 2 zwei | 3 drei |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 vier | 5 fünf | 6 sechs | 7 sieben |
| 8 acht | 9 neun | 10 zehn | 11 elf |
| 12 zwölf | | | |

**13–19** = unit + zehn: dreizehn (13), vierzehn (14), fünfzehn (15), sechzehn (16, drops the s), siebzehn (17, drops -en), achtzehn (18), neunzehn (19).

**The tens**: 20 zwanzig, 30 dreißig, 40 vierzig, 50 fünfzig, 60 sechzig, 70 siebzig, 80 achtzig, 90 neunzig, 100 (ein)hundert.

**21–99** — German says the **ones before the tens**, joined with *und*:
- 21 = einundzwanzig (one-and-twenty)
- 34 = vierunddreißig (four-and-thirty)
- 58 = achtundfünfzig
- 99 = neunundneunzig

Use numbers for your age: *Ich bin zwölf Jahre alt.* (I am twelve years old.)

notes.heading: ⚠️ Pronunciation & Special Letters
notes.body:
German spelling is very regular — once you know the sounds, you can read almost any word aloud correctly.

**Special letters:**
| Letter | Sound | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ä | like e in bed | Mädchen (girl) |
| ö | like i in bird (rounded lips) | schön (beautiful) |
| ü | say ee with tightly rounded lips | München (Munich) |
| ß (Eszett / scharfes S) | like ss | Straße (street), Fuß (foot) |

The two dots (ä, ö, ü) are called an **Umlaut**. In Switzerland ß is not used — people write *Strasse* with ss instead.

**Key consonant sounds:**
- **w** = English v: *Wasser* (water)
- **v** = English f: *Vater* (father)
- **s** at the start = English z: *sieben* (seven)
- **z** = ts: *zehn* (ten)
- **j** = English y: *ja* (yes)
- **sch** = English sh: *Schule* (school)
- **ch** = a soft hiss after e/i (ich), or a throaty sound after a/o/u (Bach)
- **ei** = eye (*mein*), **ie** = ee (*viel*) — do not mix them up!

notes.heading: 💡 Cognates & International Words
notes.body:
English and German are related languages, so thousands of words look and mean almost the same — these are called **cognates**, and they are free vocabulary:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| das Haus | house |
| die Maus | mouse |
| der Name | name |
| der Apfel | apple |
| der Bruder | brother |
| das Wasser | water |
| die Mutter | mother |
| der Winter | winter |
| kalt / warm | cold / warm |

There are also many **international words**: das Telefon, der Computer, die Musik, der Sport, das Restaurant, das Baby.

⚠️ **Common mistake — false friends:** some words look familiar but mean something different:
- **bekommen** = to receive (NOT to become — that is *werden*)
- **bald** = soon (NOT bald — that is *kahl*)
- **Gift** = poison (NOT a present — that is *das Geschenk*)
- **Chef** = boss (NOT a cook — that is *der Koch*)

Trust cognates, but always check suspicious ones in a dictionary!

flashcards.definition: Good day / hello (a polite greeting used during the day)
flashcards.example: Guten Tag, Frau Müller! — Good day, Mrs Müller!
Tschüss, bis morgen! — Bye, see you tomorrow!

flashcards.definition: What is your name? (literally: What are you called?)
flashcards.example: Hallo, wie heißt du? — Hello, what is your name?

flashcards.definition: My name is... (literally: I am called...)
flashcards.example: Ich heiße Max. — My name is Max.
Woher kommst du? Ich komme aus England. — Where do you come from? I come from England.
Ich wohne in London. — I live in London.
Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland. — Berlin is the capital of Germany.

flashcards.definition: Switzerland (a feminine country name — it keeps its article)
flashcards.example: Ich komme aus der Schweiz. — I come from Switzerland.

flashcards.definition: twenty-one (German says the ones before the tens)
flashcards.example: Mein Bruder ist einundzwanzig Jahre alt. — My brother is twenty-one years old.

flashcards.definition: the sharp-s letter, pronounced like ss
flashcards.example: Die Straße ist lang. — The street is long.

flashcards.definition: the two dots above a, o, u that change their sound (ä, ö, ü)
flashcards.example: Müller wohnt in München. — Müller lives in Munich.
Das deutsche Alphabet hat auch ä, ö, ü und ß. — The German alphabet also has ä, ö, ü and ß.

questions.explanation: Guten Tag is the standard polite daytime greeting, literally good day. Good evening is Guten Abend and goodbye is Auf Wiedersehen.

questions.stem: Which word is an informal way to say bye to a friend?
questions.explanation: Tschüss is the casual goodbye used with friends and family. Auf Wiedersehen is formal, and Guten Morgen / Gute Nacht are greetings, not goodbyes.

questions.stem: What is someone asking when they say Wie heißt du?
questions.explanation: Wie heißt du? literally means What are you called? — it is how you ask someone's name. Where you live would be Wo wohnst du?

questions.stem: Which country is NOT one of the three main D-A-CH countries?
questions.explanation: D-A-CH stands for Deutschland, Austria (Österreich) and Switzerland (Confoederatio Helvetica = die Schweiz). Dänemark (Denmark) is not a German-speaking country.
Sieben is 7. Sechs is 6, siebzehn is 17 and siebzig is 70 — the similar forms all build on the same root.

questions.stem: How do you say I live in Berlin in German?
questions.explanation: To live somewhere uses the verb wohnen: ich wohne in + town. Ich komme aus Berlin means I come from Berlin, and ich heiße gives your name.

questions.stem: Which is the correct reply to Woher kommst du?
questions.explanation: Woher kommst du? asks where you come from, so the answer uses kommen: Ich komme aus England. Ich wohne in Manchester answers Wo wohnst du? instead.

questions.stem: How do you say 43 in German?
questions.explanation: German numbers between 21 and 99 put the ones first: dreiundvierzig = three-and-forty = 43. Vierunddreißig would be 34 — the digits swapped.

questions.stem: Which German letter combination is pronounced like the English sh in ship?
questions.explanation: German sch sounds exactly like English sh, as in Schule (school) or Fisch (fish). Ch is a hissing or throaty sound, and German does not use the spelling sh.

questions.stem: A friend asks Wie geht es dir? What is the most natural reply?
questions.explanation: Wie geht es dir? means How are you?, so the natural answer is Mir geht es gut, danke. (I am fine, thank you.) The other options answer completely different questions.

questions.stem: Which German word is a cognate of the English word brother?
questions.explanation: Der Bruder means brother — English and German are related, so many family words look alike. Der Vater is father and die Schwester is sister.
With ich, regular verbs take the ending -e: ich wohne. -st goes with du, -t goes with er/sie/es, and the -en form is the infinitive, which never follows ich.

questions.stem: Ich bekomme ein Geschenk — what does bekommen mean here? Watch out, it is a false friend!
questions.explanation: Bekommen means to receive, not to become — to become is werden in German. This is one of the most famous false friends between the two languages.

questions.stem: In Switzerland, how is the ß in Straße usually written?
choices: Straße is never written in Switzerland
questions.explanation: Swiss German does not use the ß at all — words like Straße are spelled with a double s: Strasse. In Germany and Austria both Straße and the ss spelling are understood.

questions.stem: You meet your teacher, Herr Braun, in the corridor. Which greeting is most appropriate?
choices: Guten Tag, Herr Braun. Wie geht es Ihnen?
questions.explanation: Teachers are addressed formally in German-speaking countries: Guten Tag plus the formal Wie geht es Ihnen? (with Sie/Ihnen, not dir). Tschüss and Hi are too casual for this situation.
